1.o: In the close of the foregoing book (with which this is connected as a continuation of the same history) we had Saul's exit; he went down slain to the pit, though he was the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. We are now to look towards the rising sun, and to enquire where David is, and what he is doing. In this chapter we have, I. Tidings brought him to Ziklag of the death of Saul and Jonathan, by an Amalekite, who undertook to give him a particular narrative of it, ver. 1-10. II.
1.i: David hears of Saul and Jonathan's deaths at Gilboa and writes a lament, grieving even for his enemy.
1.p: Lord, You teach us to honor even our enemies. Give us tender hearts, and comfort those who grieve. Amen.
1.l: Remember something good about someone who has hurt you, and say a kind prayer for them.
q: David mourned for the man who hunted him. What would it take for you to remember the good in someone who hurt you?

2.o: David had paid due respect to the memory of Saul his prince and Jonathan his friend, and what he did was as much his praise as theirs; he is now considering what is to be done next. Saul is dead, now therefore David arise. I. By direction from God he went up to Hebron, and was there anointed king, ver. 1-4. II. He returned thanks to the men of Jabesh-Gilead for burying Saul, ver. 5-7. III. Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, is set up in opposition to him, ver. 8-11. IV.
2.i: David moves to Hebron, is crowned king of Judah, and years later all the tribes anoint him king of Israel.
2.p: Lord, You keep Your promises in Your time. Help us to wait on You. Amen.
2.l: Ask God for guidance before you make a big decision today, and then wait for His answer.
q: David waited seven years to be king over all Israel. What are you waiting for with patience?

3.o: The battle between Joab and Abner did not end the controversy between the two houses of Saul and David, but it is in this chapter working towards a period. Here is, I. The gradual advance of David's interest, ver. 1. II. The building up of his family, ver. 2-5. III. Abner's quarrel with Ish-bosheth, and his treaty with David, ver. 6-12. IV. The preliminaries settled, ver. 13-16. V. Abner's undertaking and attempt to bring Israel over to David, ver. 17-21. VI.
3.s: Abner, Joab, and the Divided House
3.i: Second Samuel 3 and 4 tell how David's path to the throne ran through two murders he did not order.
3.p: Lord, You hate injustice, even when it seems to serve Your purposes. Keep our hands clean, and bring peace to divided houses. Amen.
3.l: Choose today not to take revenge, even when you think someone deserves it.
q: David's marriage alliance later brought him grief and shame. What advantage have you taken that quietly cost more than you thought?

4.o: When Abner was slain David was at a loss for a friend to perfect the reduction of those tribes that were yet in Ish-bosheth's interest. Which way to adopt for the accomplishment of it he could not tell; but here Providence brings it about by the removal of Ish-bosheth. I. Two of his own servants slew him, and brought his head to David, ver. 1-8. II. David, instead of rewarding them, put them to death for what they had done, ver. 9-12.
4.s: Abner, Joab, and the Divided House
4.i: Second Samuel 3 and 4 tell how David's path to the throne ran through two murders he did not order.
4.p: Lord, You hate injustice, even when it seems to serve Your purposes. Keep our hands clean, and bring peace to divided houses. Amen.
4.l: Choose today not to take revenge, even when you think someone deserves it.
q: David's marriage alliance later brought him grief and shame. What advantage have you taken that quietly cost more than you thought?

5.o: How far Abner's deserting the house of Saul, his murder, and the murder of Ish-bosheth, might contribute to the perfecting of the revolution, and the establishing of David as king over all Israel, does not appear; but, it should seem, that happy change followed presently thereupon, which in this chapter we have an account of. Here is, I. David anointed king by all the tribes, ver. 1-5. II. Making himself master of the strong-hold of Zion, ver. 6-10. III.
5.i: David moves to Hebron, is crowned king of Judah, and years later all the tribes anoint him king of Israel.
5.p: Lord, You keep Your promises in Your time. Help us to wait on You. Amen.
5.l: Ask God for guidance before you make a big decision today, and then wait for His answer.
q: David waited seven years to be king over all Israel. What are you waiting for with patience?

6.o: The obscurity of the ark, during the reign of Saul, had been as great a grievance to Israel as the insults of the Philistines. David, having humbled the Philistines and mortified them in gratitude for that favour, and in pursuance of his designs for the public welfare, is here bringing up the ark to his own city, that it might be near him, and be an ornament and strength to his new foundation. Here is, I. An attempt to do it, which failed and miscarried. The design was well laid, ver. 1, 2. But, 1.
6.i: David brings the ark to Jerusalem, first on a cart that ends in tragedy, then carried by the priests with rejoicing.
6.p: Lord, You are holy and near. Teach us to worship You with joy and reverence. Amen.
6.l: Dance or sing a song of joy to God today, even if you feel silly.
q: David learned to do things God's way. Where do you need to do the right thing the right way?

7.o: Still the ark is David's care as well as his joy. In this chapter we have, I. His consultation with Nathan about building a house for it; he signifies his purpose to do it (ver. 1, 2) and Nathan approves his purpose, ver. 3. II. His communion with God about it. 1. A gracious message God sent him about it, accepting his purpose, countermanding the performance, and promising him an entail of blessings upon his family, ver. 4-17. 2.
7.s: A House for the Lord, and a House for David
7.i: David wants to build a temple, but God says through Nathan that He will build David a house, a family that will last forever.
7.p: Lord, You build houses that last. Thank You for Your promise through David. Amen.
7.l: Think of something you have wanted to do for God. Ask Him if He has something even better.
q: David wanted to give to God, and God gave first. How have you seen that?

8.o: David having sought first the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof, settling the ark as soon as he was himself well settled, we are here told how all other things were added to him. Here is an account, I. Of his conquests. He triumphed, 1. Over the Philistines, ver. 1. 2. Over the Moabites, ver. 2. 3. Over the king of Zobah, ver. 3, 4. 4. Over the Syrians, ver. 5-8, 13. 5. Over the Edomites, ver. 14. II.
8.s: David's Victories and a Shaved Delegation
8.i: Second Samuel 8 and 10 summarize David's wars and one very bad misunderstanding that started another.
8.p: Lord, You give victory in Your time. Keep us from fear, and teach us to receive kindness gratefully. Amen.
8.l: When someone offers kindness today, accept it as kindness before you look for a bad reason behind it.
q: Sending condolences was a customary kindness between allies. Whose loss could you acknowledge this week?

9.o: The only thing recorded in this chapter is the kindness David showed to Jonathan's seed for his sake. I. The kind enquiry he made after the remains of the house of Saul, and his discovery of Mephibosheth, ver. 1-4. II. The kind reception he gave to Mephibosheth, when he was brought to him, ver. 5-8. III. The kind provision he made for him and his, ver. 9-13.
9.s: A Place at the King's Table
9.i: King David, remembering his promise to Jonathan, found Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth, restored his land, and gave him a permanent place at the royal table.
9.p: Lord, You have invited us to Your table, though we cannot walk straight. Thank You for grace. Amen.
9.l: Invite someone who is often left out to sit with you at lunch or play with you today.
q: David showed kindness for the sake of someone else. Who has shown you kindness that you did not earn?

10.o: This chapter gives us an account of a war David has with the Ammonites and the Syrians their allies, with the occasion and success of it. I. David sent a friendly embassy to Hanun king of the Ammonites, ver. 1, 2. II. He, upon a base surmise that it was ill intended, abused David's ambassadors, ver. 3, 4. III. David resenting it (ver. 5), and the Ammonites prepared for war against him, ver. 6. IV. David carried the war into their country, sent against them.
10.s: David's Victories and a Shaved Delegation
10.i: Second Samuel 8 and 10 summarize David's wars and one very bad misunderstanding that started another.
10.p: Lord, You give victory in Your time. Keep us from fear, and teach us to receive kindness gratefully. Amen.
10.l: When someone offers kindness today, accept it as kindness before you look for a bad reason behind it.
q: Sending condolences was a customary kindness between allies. Whose loss could you acknowledge this week?

11.o: What David said of the mournful report of Saul's death may more fitly be applied to the sad story of this chapter, the adultery and murder David was guilty of.—"Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon." We wish we could draw a veil over it, and that it might never be known, might never be said, that David did such things as are here recorded of him. But it cannot, it must not, be concealed.
11.i: The first verses of this chapter are a chain: a king out of his place, an idle afternoon, a wandering eye.
11.p: Lord, You see everything and You forgive the repentant. Keep us from hiding our wrongs, and heal those who have been hurt by the powerful. Amen.
11.l: Ask a grown-up to read this chapter with you, and talk about why hiding a wrong only makes it bigger.
q: Where does your own idle time tend to lead you?

12.o: The foregoing chapter gave us the account of David's sin; this gives us the account of his repentance. Though he fell, he was not utterly cast down, but, by the grace of God, recovered himself, and found mercy with God. Here is, I. His conviction, by a message Nathan brought him from God, which was a parable that obliged him to condemn himself (ver. 1-6), and the application of the parable, in which Nathan charged him with the sin (ver. 7-9) and pronounced sentence upon him,, ver. 10-12. II.
12.i: Nathan tells David a story about a rich man and a poor man's lamb, and David realizes the story is about himself.
12.p: Lord, search us and show us where we have gone wrong. Give us clean hearts. Amen.
12.l: If you have done something wrong, say sorry to God and to the person you hurt.
q: David could see the wrong in someone else but not in himself. When is it hard for you to see your own faults?

13.o: The righteous God had lately told David, by Nathan the prophet, that, to chastise him for his son in the matter of Uriah, he would "raise up evil against him out of his own house," (ch. xii. 11). And here, in the very next chapter, we find the evil beginning to rise; henceforward he was followed with one trouble after another, which made the latter part of his reign less glorious and pleasant than the former part.
13.i: Second Samuel 13 records one of the darkest stories in the Bible, in which the abuse of a princess starts a chain of family violence.
13.p: Lord, You see the wronged and the silent. Make us people who protect the vulnerable, and heal those who carry deep wounds. Amen.
13.l: Ask a grown-up to talk with you about what to do if someone you trust hurts you, and who to tell.
q: David was fond of his children and acted too late. Where have you let something wrong go unaddressed because of love?

14.o: How Absalom threw himself out of his royal father's protection and favour we read in the foregoing chapter, which left him an exile, outlawed, and proscribed; in this chapter we have the arts that were used to bring him and his father together again, and how, at last, it was done, which is here recorded to show the folly of David in sparing him and indulging him in his wickedness, for which he was soon after severely corrected by his unnatural rebellion. I.
14.i: Second Samuel 14 uses a made-up story to reach a king's heart, and contains one of the Bible's best lines about God's way of bringing people home.
14.p: Lord, You do not want anyone to stay estranged. Show us how to make peace, and to bring home those who are far from us. Amen.
14.l: If you have been waiting to make up with someone, take one small step today.
q: A parable lets someone hear a truth they would not accept if it were pointed straight at them. Who might you need to approach sideways with a story?

15.o: Absalom's name signifies "the peace of his father," yet he proves his greatest trouble; so often are we disappointed in our expectations from the creature. The sword entailed upon David's house had hitherto been among his children, but now it begins to be drawn against himself, with this aggravation, that he may thank himself for it, for, had he done justice upon the murderer, he would have prevented the traitor.
15.s: David Climbs the Mount of Olives
15.i: When Absalom's revolt forced him out of Jerusalem, David wept his way up the Mount of Olives, trusting God to decide his future, and was followed by a loyal foreign soldier.
15.p: Lord, You keep faith with us in our worst days. Make us loyal friends, and keep our hearts humble. Amen.
15.l: Be a friend like Ittai today. Tell someone who is having a hard time, I am staying with you.
q: Ittai, a foreigner, stayed loyal when everyone else left. Who has stayed with you, and whom could you stay with?

16.o: In the close of the foregoing chapter we left David flying from Jerusalem, and Absalom entering into it; in this chapter, I. We are to follow David in his melancholy flight; and there we find him, 1. Cheated by Ziba, ver. 1-4. 2. Cursed by Shimei, which he bears with wonderful patience, ver. 5-14. II. We are to meet Absalom in his triumphant entry; and there we find him, 1. Cheated by Hushai, ver. 15-19. 2. Counselled by Ahithophel to go in unto his father's concubines, ver. 20-23.
16.i: Second Samuel 16 shows David leaving Jerusalem, a king humbled, and how he handled being cursed on the road.
16.p: Lord, You see our trouble. Teach us to bear insults with humility, and to trust You to set things right. Amen.
16.l: When someone says something unkind to you today, take a breath and answer calmly, or not at all.
q: A humble spirit turns reproaches into reproofs. What criticism have you refused to learn from because of who said it?

17.o: The contest between David and Absalom is now hasting towards a crisis. It must be determined by the sword, and preparation is made accordingly in this chapter. I. Absalom calls a council of war, in which Ahithophel urges despatch (ver. 1-4), but Hushai recommends deliberation (ver. 5-13); and Hushai's counsel is agreed to (ver. 14), for vexation at which Ahithophel hangs himself, ver. 23. II. Secret intelligence is sent to David (but with much difficulty) of their proceedings, ver. 15-21. III.
17.s: Beds, Bowls and Honey at Mahanaim
17.i: When David fled from Absalom and reached Mahanaim, three generous men brought him and his weary people beds, bowls, food and honey.
17.p: Lord, thank You for friends who see our needs. Make us generous, and ready with open hands. Amen.
17.l: Look for someone who is tired or having a rough time today, and bring them something: a snack, a note, or a hug.
q: Three people brought what David needed before he asked. Who might need your generosity before they ask?

18.o: This chapter puts a period to Absalom's rebellion and life, and so makes way for David to his throne again, whither the next chapter brings him back in peace and triumph. We have here, I. David's preparations to engage the rebels, ver. 1-5. II. The total defeat of Absalom's party and their dispersion, ver. 6-8. III. The death of Absalom, and his burial, ver. 9-18. IV. The bringing of the tidings to David, who tarried at Mahanaim, ver. 19-32. V. His bitter lamentation for Absalom, ver. 33.
18.i: King David won the battle against his rebellious son Absalom, then wept over his death, because he was first of all a father.
18.p: Lord, You love us even when we turn away. Heal the grief of every parent, and teach us to love as You do. Amen.
18.l: Tell a parent or someone who cares for you that you love them, today, with words.
q: David loved the son who had rebelled against him. Whom do you find hardest to love, and what does that cost you?

19.o: We left David's army in triumph and yet David himself in tears: now here we have, I. His return to himself, by the persuasion of Joab, ver. 1-8. II. His return to his kingdom from his present banishment. 1. The men of Israel were forward of themselves to bring him back, ver. 9, 10. 2. The men of Judah were dealt with by David's agents to do it (ver. 11-14) and did it, ver. 15. III. At the king's coming over Jordan, Shimei's treason is pardoned (ver. 16-23), Mephibosheth's failure is excused (ver.
19.i: David returned across the Jordan, forgave a man who had cursed him, and honored the old man who fed him in exile.
19.p: Lord, teach us to forgive those who hurt us and to honor those who help us. Amen.
19.l: Do something kind for someone who helped you long ago. Say thank you, or give a small gift.
q: David showed mercy to the man who cursed him and gratitude to the man who fed him. Which one is harder for you?

20.o: How do the clouds return after the rain! No sooner is one of David's troubles over than another arises, as it were out of the ashes of the former, wherein the threatening is fulfilled, that the sword should never depart from his house. I. Before he reaches Jerusalem a new rebellion is raised by Sheba, ver. 1, 2. II. His first work, when he comes to Jerusalem, is to condemn his concubines to perpetual imprisonment, ver. 3. III.
20.i: Second Samuel 20 describes the last small rebellion of David's troubled years, and a city saved by one speech.
20.p: Lord, give us wisdom to speak peace and the courage to say it. Make us peacemakers in our cities and homes. Amen.
20.l: Use words, not force, to settle a disagreement today. Speak calmly, and listen.
q: A newly set bone needs time to knit. What relationship are you rushing past the healing stage?

21.o: The date of the events of this chapter is uncertain. I incline to think that they happened as they are here placed, after Absalom's and Sheba's rebellion, and towards the latter end of David's reign. That the battles with the Philistines, mentioned here, were long after the Philistines were subdued, appears by comparing 1 Chron. xviii. 1 with xx. 4. The numbering of the people was just before the fixing of the place of the temple (as appears 1 Chron. xxii.
21.i: Second Samuel 21 gathers three hard stories: a famine, a mother's faithful watch, and the war with the giants.
21.p: Lord, You keep promises across generations. Teach us to honor our word, and bless those who keep faith in hard places. Amen.
21.l: Keep a promise today that you have been putting off, even a small one.
q: A wrong done long before was only now reckoned. What old promise or debt are you hoping stays forgotten?

22.o: This chapter is a psalm, a psalm of praise; we find it afterwards inserted among David's psalms (Ps. xviii.) with some little variation. We have it here as it was first composed for his own closed and his own harp; but there we have it as it was afterwards delivered to the chief musician for the service of the church, a second edition with some amendments; for, though it was calculated primarily for David's case, yet it might indifferently serve the devotion of others, in giving thanks for their deliverances; or…
22.i: Second Samuel 22 is David's long song of thanksgiving, nearly the same as Psalm 18.
22.p: Lord, You are my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer. I will praise You among the nations and sing to Your name. Amen.
22.l: Write or say your own short song of thanks to God, using one of David's lines such as The Lord is my rock.
q: Men begin in kindness but do not finish. Where has God finished something you could not?

23.o: The historian is now drawing towards a conclusion of David's reign, and therefore gives us an account here, I. Of some of his last words, which he spoke by inspiration, and which seem to have reference to his seed that was to be for evermore, spoken of in the close of the foregoing chapter, ver. 1-7. II. Of the great men, especially the military men, that were employed under him, the first three (ver. 8-17), two of the next three (ver. 18-23), and then the thirty, ver. 24-39.
23.s: Water from the Well at Bethlehem
23.i: Three of David's mighty men risk their lives to bring him water from Bethlehem, and David pours it out as an offering.
23.p: Lord, thank You for those who sacrifice for us. Teach us to honor their gifts and to give them to You. Amen.
23.l: Thank someone today who has done something for you that cost them, and show your thanks with a kind act.
q: David wouldn't drink what cost his men so much. What do you treat as too precious to waste?

24.o: The last words of David, which we read in the chapter before, were admirably good, but in this chapter we read of some of his last works, which were none of the best; yet he repented, and did his first works again, and so he finished well. We have here, I. His sin, which was numbering the people in the pride of his heart, ver. 1-9. II. His conviction of the sin, and repentance for it, ver. 10. III. The judgment inflicted upon him for it, ver. 11-15. IV. The staying of the judgment, ver. 16, 17. V.
24.i: David buys Araunah's threshing floor to build an altar and stop the plague, refusing to give God what costs him nothing.
24.p: Lord, You gave Your Son for us. Teach us to give to You what costs us something. Amen.
24.l: Give God something today that costs you something, like your time or something you like.
q: David refused a free gift to give to God. What have you given God that cost you something?
